en: The Collected Explanations of the Treatise by Shi Dunlun, Volume Seventy-Eight.
Below this is the sixth section: the inquiry of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva regarding the meaning of the various stages (*bhūmi*). Within this:
First, the core thesis is indicated by citing the sūtra;
next, the text itself is formally quoted.
Regarding the former, it says: "Furthermore, based on the vehicle (yāna), one provisionally establishes and explains the Mahāyāna as it truly is," and so forth.
Based on the Mahāyāna, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth are provisionally established in relation to the levels of spiritual practice.
Within the actual scriptural citations,
the meaning of these various stages is first correctly elucidated through a series of questions and answers.
Regarding the subsequent request to establish the title of the sutra and the benefits gained by the assembly,
there are two parts in the preceding section: first,
the prose (long-form), and second, the verses (repeated stanzas).
The prose section consists of four parts:
first, the exposition of the meaning of the stages;
second, the exposition of the dharmas to be studied within those stages.
Third, the discrimination of the afflictions existing within the stages (*bhūmi*).
Fourth, the discrimination of the intended meaning of teaching the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Regarding the first, the discrimination of the afflictions within the stages, there are six [sections].
First, the summary of the meaning;
second, the explanation of the names of the stages;
third, the analysis of the factors to be eliminated within each stage.
Fourth, the analysis of the qualities of purity common to all stages.
Fifth, the clarification that bodhisattvas are superior due to four conditions.
Sixth, the analysis of the bodhisattva’s practice of the great vows.
At the beginning, there is first the question and then the answer.
Regarding the inquiry concerning Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
he was formerly called Guanshiyin.
This is an error by the translator.
Furthermore, in the older translations of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra*, he is named Avalokiteśvara;
this was merely based on the characters for "World-Sound" (*lokasvara*).
Now, according to the Sanskrit language, the name is translated as Avalokiteśvara.
There are two aspects to this:
first, the inquiry into purity.
This consists of two parts:
the section on questions and the section on answers. In the answers, there is first a general response, followed by a detailed explanation through specific inquiries.
Within this, first, the four kinds of purity may be understood through their explanation;
next, the inclusion within the eleven divisions is explained,
meaning that the eleven stages are designated as the eleven divisions.
Within each stage (*bhūmi*),
first the fulfillment of its own constituent parts is clarified;
second, the non-fulfillment of the part of further advancement is clarified.
Regarding the phrase "first, on the stage of practice through resolute belief, one thoroughly cultivates the ten dharma-practices," Jing says:
"The ten dharma-practices are [the acts of] writing, upholding, making offerings, reading for oneself, and giving to others."
Furthermore, even while still on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), one may look up and study the practices of the ten grounds,
which is called "the ten dharma-practices being excellently cultivated," and so forth.
Tai says:

Because one previously cultivated the patience of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-kṣānti*) based on the ten types of practices, such as writing and upholding [the Dharma], prior to the stages (*bhūmi*),
one enters the portion of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is explained thus:
The ten perfections are called the ten dharmas.
When a Bodhisattva on the third stage has not yet been able to relinquish attachment to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and attachment to the Dharma,
this constitutes an obstruction to the fourth stage.
Before the name is attained, it is already perfected;
in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this is called the obstacle of pride regarding the understanding of the Dharma.
This continues until this portion is perfected.
Although the fourth stage is perfected,
one who has not yet been able to observe the principles of the truths as they truly are has not attained the contemplation of the truths of the fifth stage.
Furthermore, regarding those who have not yet abandoned the mind that turns its back [on saṃsāra] and have not yet cultivated skillful means and so forth:
on the fifth stage, they penetrate the suffering of birth and death and are able to enter it constantly;
they also penetrate the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Yet they do not seek it quickly;
these two skillful means have not yet been attained on the fourth stage,
and are intended for those below it.
Although the fifth stage is perfected,
one is not yet able to observe the flow of birth and death as it truly is;
at the sixth stage, one is able to observe the flow of dependent origination.
It is not attained on the fifth stage.
Furthermore, because one has developed much weariness toward that [stage], one is unable to dwell extensively in the mental attention to signlessness (*animitta-manasikāra*).
On the seventh stage, one enters long-term mental attention to signlessness within true suchness (*tathatā*).
Although one does not enter [the signless] continuously in the sixth stage, one is able to dwell extensively in the mental application of the signless (*animitta-manasikāra*).
This is because Bodhisattvas in the fifth stage generate much weariness toward the suffering of birth and death,
and thus cannot dwell extensively in the mental application of the signless.
If one is unable to dwell in the frequent cultivation of the mental attention on the signless (animitta-manasikāra) without deficiency or interruption,
and has not yet attained the long-term entry into true contemplation of the seventh stage,
one is still unable to relinquish effort within the dwelling in the signless.
On the seventh stage, one has not yet attained the signlessness and effortlessness of the eighth stage,
nor has one yet attained mastery over signs. Thus,
although the Bodhisattva on the eighth stage still exerts effort regarding the signs of conventional truth, [he is free from effort regarding ultimate truth].
Furthermore, mastery according to one's capacity has not yet been attained on the seventh stage.

This clarifies that one has not yet attained the quality of the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage regarding the distinctions in synonyms, characteristics, and etymological definitions.
The "different names" refer to the unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
The "various characteristics" refer to the unimpededness regarding meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the "distinctions in terminology," it refers to attaining great mastery in the teaching of the Dharma through all categories of unimpeded expression.
The unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition is not yet attained in the eighth stage;
this is what is meant by "not yet being able."
As for those who have not yet attained the manifest realization and experience of the perfectly complete Dharmakāya:
while Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage have exhausted all coarse afflictions and their Dharmakāya is perfected,
those of the ninth stage have not yet attained it.
One who has not yet attained the sublime wisdom and sublime vision that are unattached and unimpeded with respect to all objects of knowledge has not yet attained the fruit of Buddhahood;
the fruit of Buddhahood is free from the afflictive obscurations.
Therefore, it is called the wondrous wisdom of non-attachment;
because it is free from the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
it is called the unimpeded wondrous vision.
The ten stages have not yet been attained.
From "in order to cause those below" onwards,
it clarifies the attainment of the Buddha’s perfection.
Question:
According to the *Mūlaparivarta-sūtra*, the eleventh stage is called the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*).
Why, then, is it stated here that the Tathāgata-stage is the eleventh stage?
The commentary states:
There are two meanings.
First, the separate discussion of cause and effect.
Only the wondrous enlightenment is named the Stage of Wondrous Arrival,
as explained herein. Second,
the causes are subsumed under their corresponding fruits.
The stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and the stage of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) are both termed the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
As stated in that sutra,
since there are these two meanings, [they are so designated].
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Second, the explanation of the meaning of the stage name:
"accomplishing the great purpose."
This is precisely the accomplishment of one's own benefit and the benefit of others;
it is called the fulfillment of the great purpose.
It is the attainment of the unprecedented supramundane mind.
Upon first attaining non-conceptual wisdom, one gives rise to joy.
Vasubandhu, taking this meaning from within [the text], explains the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) as follows:
"One accomplishes the unsurpassed benefit of oneself and others."
Because one experiences great joy upon first realizing the state of a noble one (ārya),
it is called the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi);
it is named according to its essential meaning.
Being far removed from all subtle transgressions of the precepts is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
A deliberate transgression is termed "gross," while an inadvertent transgression is termed "subtle."
First, one is free from intentional transgressions;
second, on this stage, one is free from errors.
Therefore, it is said that one remains far removed from even subtle violations of the precepts.
The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) also adopts this meaning.
Its commentary there states:
"It is apart from the defilements of afflictions that give rise to the transgression of precepts through a deluded mind."
Because they are fully endowed with pure precepts,
they are named "Stainless" (Vimalā). Furthermore,
they derive their name from this meaning.
Regarding the phrase "from that up to the Radiant Stage":
on the third stage, one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as well as the retention of what has been heard (*śrutadhāraṇī*).
This retention of what has been heard is itself a specific differentiation within meditative concentration.
Because one can produce the light of wisdom by relying on these various meditative concentrations,
it is called the "Radiant Stage" (*Prabhākarī-bhūmi*). Here,
"producing" (*prabhā*) carries the sense of "causing to arise."
"Light" has the meaning of "fruit.
The name is formed by combining "cause" and "fruit.
The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) says:
Regarding the statement that "the stage is called Illumination (Prabhākari) because the Dharma appears through the light of hearing, reflection, and cultivation":
it is named the Stage of Illumination because the three types of wisdom shine forth.
This name is derived directly from the fruit of the wisdom produced by those [three practices].
Regarding the factors of enlightenment attained by him which lead to the stage named "Blazing Wisdom" (Arciṣmatī):
afflictions are like firewood,
and wisdom is like a flame.
On the fourth stage, the fire of the Path burns the fuel of afflictions;
as both the phenomenon and its metaphor are thus designated,
it is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
The treatise also adopts this meaning and directly names it the "Blazing Ground" (Arciṣmatī).

It is called the "Extremely Difficult to Conquer Ground" (Sudurjayā) because, in that very stage, the superior wisdoms regarding the ultimate and the conventional are in conflict and fail to achieve their aim. This refers to the fifth ground.
Because it is only through many hardships that one can cause [the factors] to arise together,
it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" stage (Dūraṃgamā bhūmi).
It is named according to its meaning.
The *Dilun shi* (Commentary on the Treatise on the Stages) states:
"Because one attains supramundane wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that can deliver those who are difficult to deliver,
it is called the 'Difficult to Conquer' Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*)."
Regarding "one who observes the flow of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) as they manifest before them":
subsequently, wisdom manifests and observes dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
Furthermore, it is only when one has extensively cultivated mental attention (manasikāra) toward the signless (animitta) that [this wisdom] manifests before one.
Non-conceptual wisdom manifests only after much cultivation and effort;
because these two types of wisdom manifest [simultaneously],
the sixth stage is named the "Manifest" (Abhimukhī) Stage.
The name is derived from its meaning.
The *Dichilun* (Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra) commentary states:
"In the practice of Prajñāpāramitā, there are intervals during which great wisdom manifests."
It is called the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Because non-conceptual wisdom does not continue uninterruptedly,
it is said that Prajñāpāramitā has intervals.
Because mental attention (*manasikāra*) arises only [at this stage],
it is called "the manifestation of great wisdom.
Because one is able to enter into realization from afar, it is named the "Far-Reaching Stage" (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*).
Beginning from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh,
one practices the signless conduct (*animitta-caryā*) for one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*;
only then does one attain uninterrupted realization and enter the signless state.
Adjacent to that eighth stage of purity is the stage named Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching).
The eighth stage is called the Stage of Purity because it is free from the fault of effortful application (*abhisamskāra*).
The *Dilun* commentary states:
"When the application of effort in the practice of signlessness is thoroughly cultivated to its ultimate limit,
one is able to transcend both the mundane path and the supramundane path of the two vehicles."
Therefore, it is named "Far-Reaching.
In the preceding six stages, although one also cultivates signless practice, it cannot be sustained continuously;
thus, they cannot be called "Excellent."
Because it is immediately followed by the seventh stage,
it is called "well-cultivated.
This refers to the various practices initiated during the preceding seven stages.
Furthermore, there is the stage of effortful application (*sābhoga*).
Now, the seventh stage is at the very end of the practice of effortful application;
therefore, it is called the "culmination of effortful application."
In the first three stages, one cultivates generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration,
which are identical to those of the mundane world.
In the fourth stage, one cultivates the factors of the path.
The fifth stage consists of the contemplation of the truths,
and the sixth stage consists of dependent origination;
these are identical to the supramundane paths of the two vehicles.
Now, having attained the seventh stage, one is able to transcend the two preceding stages;
thus it is said that one can surpass both the mundane path and the supramundane path of the two vehicles.
Therefore, it is named the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā bhūmi*).
This is also named according to its meaning:
because one reaches the state of signlessness (animitta), it is called the Immovable Ground (acalā-bhūmi);
for true gnosis (bhūtajñāna) has attained non-effortful spontaneity (anābhoga) and is thus unshakable.
Although conventional wisdom involves effortful application, it is not moved by manifest afflictions;
thus it is called "immovable. This name is also derived from its functional significance.
The *Dichilun* (Treatise on the Stages) commentary explains:
"Because the practice on the stage is able to reach full maturity, being signless and uninterrupted, it is called 'Immovable' (Acalā).
This explains "Immovable" directly in terms of true gnosis (*tattvajñāna*).

"In all its aspects, it is designated as the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī)" refers to the fact that at this stage, one possesses the wisdom that skillfully distinguishes the various categories of phenomena.
He possesses mastery in teaching the Dharma to all types of beings according to their capacities;
he is skilled in understanding and has attained vast, faultless wisdom.
It is the wisdom of understanding.
Wisdom is the essence and goodness is its meaning;
it is named according to both its essence and its meaning.
The *Dilun* explains the name [of this stage]:
through the power of non-obstruction, one preaches the Dharma and accomplishes practices for the benefit of others.
It is named the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
This directly explains the meaning of "excellent" (*sādhu*) but does not explain the meaning of "intelligence" (*mati*).
Regarding the meaning of "coarseness" (dauṣṭhulya) up until the stage called the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi):
the inherent lack of pliancy within the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of all infinite afflictive and cognitive obstructions is termed the "body of coarseness."
It is like space;
the dharmakāya realized in the ten stages is perfected,
being like a great cloud.
Because it is able to universally cover all coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya) like space,
it is called the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā).
"Dharma" refers to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
The Dharma-body is likened to clouds;
because both the phenomenon and its metaphor are presented together,
it is called the "Dharma-Cloud."
In the ancient commentary by Vasubandhu,
Dharmamitra explains that "cloud" is used as a metaphor for wisdom (*jñāna*).
This also presents both the dharma and the metaphor together;
therefore, it is called the "Dharma-Cloud" (dharmameghā) stage.
The *Dilun* commentary explains:
This refers to the Great Dharmakāya being fully endowed with mastery;
it is called the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
From "permanently severing" onwards...
The understanding of the Buddha-ground can be known from this.
Third, regarding the factors to be eliminated within the analysis of the grounds:
these consist of twenty-two types of delusion (*moha*) and eleven types of heavy impediment (*dausthulya*).
This refers to the twenty-two types of dullness (*moha-anuśaya*), which are heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) and lack of flexibility.
As the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha’s translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The twenty-two types of ignorance (*avidyā-dausthulya*) result in the four kinds of birth and death."
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* does not clarify the four kinds of ignorance;
rather, it distinguishes the four types of birth-and-death based on the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* obtained from the Southern Land.
Now, the Tripiṭaka Master has examined the Sanskrit original and found that it lacks the word "retribution" as well as the section on the four types of birth-and-death.
Therefore, it is said that there are twenty-two types of delusion (*moha*) and eleven types of gross heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Regarding these twenty-two delusions,
they were previously analyzed in relation to one another within the ten hindrances in the preceding fascicle.
Now, the characteristics will be briefly explained.
The text consists of four sections:
first, the question; second, the answer; third, the conclusion; and fourth, the acknowledgment.
In the response, regarding the two delusions of the first stage:
the first is the delusion of grasping at the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*),
which refers precisely to the two attachments to the person and to phenomena.
Second, regarding the delusion of the afflictions,
karma, and birth within the three types of defilement of the evil destinies:
this consists of two parts concerning the second stage.
First, subtle transgressions,
which are offenses committed through lapses of mindfulness;
second, various courses of karmic action.
This refers to seeing the distinctions among the three karmas and the three types of conduct.
Regarding the two delusions of the third stage:
the first is the obstruction of sensual desire.
This obstructs meditative concentration (samādhi).
Second, regarding the delusion concerning the perfection of the dhāraṇī for hearing and retaining:
from the third bhūmi onward, one has already attained qualities such as the dhāraṇī for hearing and retaining.
In the second bhūmi, it has not yet been attained;
it is named after that which obstructs it.
In the fourth bhūmi, there are two [types].
First is attachment to meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
this arises within the first three stages and obstructs the mind from entering the fourth stage through its craving for dhyāna.
Second is attachment to the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
Bodhisattvas on the third stage practice patience in seeking the Dharma because they cherish the Dharma,
as explained at length in the sutras.
Regarding the two [points] of the fifth stage:
First, one-pointed attention directed toward turning one's back on saṃsāra;
second, one-pointed attention directed toward proceeding toward nirvāṇa;
and those that arise as obstacles during the four stages, making five in total.
Regarding the two aspects of the sixth stage:
first, "directly observing the flow and transformation of all conditioned phenomena" means that in the sixth stage,
one directly contemplates the flow and transformation of all conditioned phenomena through the twelve links of dependent origination.
The obstacles not yet overcome on the fifth stage hinder entry into the sixth stage;
it is named after that which is obstructed.
Regarding the two characteristics that frequently manifest:
Although Bodhisattvas on the fifth stage both weary of and delight in [the mundane],
their weariness toward the characteristics of birth and death manifests predominantly and acts as an obstacle to the sixth stage.
The seventh stage has two [aspects].
The first is the delusion regarding the manifestation of subtle marks;
in the seventh stage, one enters for a long duration into the true contemplation of signlessness.
Although one contemplates signlessness on the sixth stage, one is not yet able to remain in it without interruption;
from time to time, subtle signs still manifest.
This capacity to obstruct birth [in the pure lands] is called delusion.
Regarding the second type, those who are deluded concerning the skillful means of the exclusively signless mental attention (*ekānta-nimitta-apraṇihita-manasikāra-upāya-mūḍha*):
although the skillful means of the mental attention of the seventh stage consists in the continuous flow of the true contemplation of the exclusively signless,
in the sixth stage one still perceives subtle signs (*sūkṣma-nimitta*) appearing before them.
That which obstructs the mental application (*manasikāra*) and skillful means (*upāya*) of the seventh stage— which are exclusively signless (*animitta*)—
is established as one further delusion (*moha*) with respect to the qualities that are obstructed.
On the eighth stage, there are two [delusions].
First, regarding those who are deluded about the effort involved in the mental attention to the signless (*animitta-manasikāra*):
although true insight (*bhūta-darśana*) continues uninterruptedly through the seventh stage, it still involves effort.
The obstacle to the eighth stage consists of two types: first, the ignorance regarding signlessness and effortlessness;
second, the ignorance regarding mastery over the practice of signs.
Regarding the latter, a bodhisattva on the eighth stage has not yet attained mastery over the effortful application of benefiting others within the sphere of conventional signs.
Self-benefit has already attained mastery through effortlessness;
this was not yet possible in the seventh stage.
It is named after that which it obstructs.
"Name" refers to mastery over the functioning of signs.
The ninth stage has two aspects:
first, regarding those who expound immeasurable teachings, this is the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
The "immeasurable dharmas, phrases, and syllables" refer to the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
The "mastery of eloquence" refers to the unimpeded knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid) and the unimpeded knowledge of ready speech (pratibhānapratisaṃvid).
The ninth stage has already been attained,
while the eighth stage has not yet been attained;
both are named according to what they obstruct.
The tenth stage has two [types of delusion]:
first, the delusion regarding great supernormal powers;
second, the delusion regarding the subtle and secret realization of entry [into the ultimate].
The great supernormal powers (mahābhijñā) constitute the fivefold Dharma-body (pañcāṅga-dharmakāya).
The subtle and secret constitutes the True Suchness Dharma-body (tathatā-dharmakāya).
One does not attain the perfection of these two Dharma-bodies until the ninth stage (navamī bhūmi).
The stage of the Tathāgata has two aspects.
First, regarding all objects of knowledge, there is an extremely subtle attachment;
this is the afflictive latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of the lowest-of-the-low grade within the conceptualization of compassion.
Second, that which is the most extremely subtle obstruction refers to the essence of the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) of the lowest-of-the-low grade within the conceptualization of compassion.
Fourth is the discernment of the qualities of universal purity throughout the stages (bhūmi).
First, the eight kinds of purity are clarified;
formerly called the "eight fruits," they are explained in detail as in the *Vihāra* chapter.
Among these, first, the purity of intention has mental attention (*manasikāra*) as its essence;
second, the purity of mind...
It takes meditative concentration as its essence;
the remaining six are easily understood.
These are all results that comprise the maturation of retribution.
This is called the purity of arising;
therefore, it does not exist in the stage of a Buddha.
Next, the distinction between that which has a superior and that which is unsurpassed is explained.
The fifth clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s birth is superior by virtue of the four conditions.
The sixth distinguishes the Bodhisattva’s practice of the various great vows;
regarding what are called "vast, wondrous, and supreme vows":
There are two explanations for this.
One explanation is that it is called a "vast vow" because it extensively transforms all sentient beings.
It is called the "Sublime Vow" because it cultivates all that is wholesome and severs all that is unwholesome.
It is named "Supreme Vow.
First, as for the explanation of the "vast vow," it is simply the vast mind.
The sublime vow is the foremost mind;
the supreme vow is the non-erroneous mind.
Regarding the four causes and conditions:
He is able to thoroughly understand the blissful dwelling of nirvāṇa and is capable of swiftly realizing it as the foremost;
yet he further relinquishes that swift realization of the blissful dwelling for the sake of the second [goal].
Third is the arousal of the mind of great aspiration without conditions or dependence;
fourth is dwelling amidst long-term suffering for the sake of benefiting others.
Although there are six sections, [the first two are combined].
The first section, which clarifies the meaning of the stages, is now complete.
From here below begins the second section, which clarifies the dharmas to be studied within those stages;
it consists of twenty-three propositions.
The excellence of cause and effect in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* arises from this.
First, the six perfections are presented as the objects of study;
second, the three trainings are used to subsume the six perfections.
It should be understood that the first three are the two types of training in higher training.
Generosity and patience are the retinue of ethical discipline (*śīla*) that assist in its accomplishment;
they are also termed "ethical discipline."
Third, the six perfections are subsumed by three kinds of provisions;
one increases these four, establishes the five aspects, and practices the ten types of dharma-practice regarding giving and the others.
Then, [the sections on] "Writing" and so forth constitute the fifth [section], which explains and establishes the six numbers.
The sixth [section] clarifies the intention for establishing the latter four perfections.
For one who has not been able to hear the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and has not well cultivated it as an object,
"hearing" refers to the act of listening,
and "object" refers to that which is taken as the focus of mental attention.
7. Distinguishing the sequence.
8. Distinguishing the categories.
9. Explaining the meaning of *pāramitā*.
10. Explaining the six corruptions that are the objects of treatment;
11. Explaining the attainment of the fruit;
12. Explaining the defiled dharmas interspersed with giving and so forth.
Thirteen, the refutation of what is not a skillful means;
fourteen, the explanation of general and specific purity.
Regarding the five aspects mentioned above:
These are the five characteristics, beginning with non-attachment,
which apply universally to the six perfections.
Based on these, the pure precepts are distinguished as being sevenfold.
First, thorough knowledge of the establishment [of the precepts];
second, thorough knowledge of renunciation;
third, being one who possesses constant ethical discipline (*śīla*).
It means constantly guarding the śīla.
As for the "four firm śīlas," it means firmly maintaining the śīla.
Regarding the five types of eternally abiding śīla:
the first is called the "precept of action" (kṛta-śīla),
and the second is called the "precept of undertaking" (samādatta-śīla).
Regarding the "sixfold śīla that constantly turns":
one interpretation says it is the *avijñapti-śīla* (unmanifest precept);
another says it is the "conforming precept" (*anuśīla*).
Seventh, regarding the training in all [precepts]:
those who purify the buddha-field through patience are first explained as those who have deep faith in cause and effect, up to and including not being frivolous.
Second, not retaliating with harm;
third, not harboring resentment;
fourth, not becoming angry when being admonished.
Fifth, not waiting for others to offer admonition;
sixth, practicing patience without being motivated by a mind stained with fear;
seventh, not abandoning [the practice] through mere mental preoccupation.
Second, there are three [aspects]: first, believing in the karmic results of actions;
second, not giving rise to anger or malice toward those who cause harm;
and third, not retaliating.
Fourth, being free from the fetter of resentment;
fifth, not becoming angry when being admonished, nor even waiting for an admonition;
sixth, acting with a mind that is not driven by fear or defilement.
Seventh, not relinquishing through the thought of [worldly] activity.
Regarding the seven types of diligence:
first, thoroughly penetrating equality so as not to exalt oneself or disparage others.
Second, possessing great power is the diligence of donning the armor.
Third, possessing great vigor is having power.
Fourth, being capable means having the capacity for endurance.

First, the aspect of being obtained through the perception of manifest activity: this refers to [the realization] that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, and so forth; because this is obtained through worldly direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is called the aspect of being obtained through manifest perception.

the suffering of oppression and so forth,
and the nature of non-self because one lacks mastery over what one does.

First, regarding the characteristic obtained through direct observation of the basis:
it refers to the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary in nature.
This is the first gate.
That there is a nature in future lives is the second.
That pure and impure karma does not perish is the third.
This refers to the dharma that is the basis for reliance and that which is to be inferred.
Regarding the phrase "because that basis, characterized by coarse and impermanent nature, is presently perceivable":
first, there is this coarse impermanence of death and birth.
It must rely upon subtle momentary impermanence;
since there exists a coarse nature of impermanence as that which depends [upon it],
we know for certain that subtle momentary impermanence must exist.
Regarding the phrase "because the various distinctions among sentient beings are observed to arise based on their various karmas":
it is directly perceived that the various sufferings and pleasures of sentient beings are obtained in dependence upon their wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Now, seeing that sentient beings further create good and evil deeds,
one can infer by comparison that there is the nature of suffering and happiness in other worlds;
for it is observed that the pleasure or pain of sentient beings is currently obtainable based upon their pure or impure karma.
First, the characteristic established by direct perception: one perceives that the pleasure and pain experienced by sentient beings depend upon wholesome and unwholesome karma;
by inference, one knows that pure and impure karma must necessarily produce their respective fruits without fail or destruction.

Third, the characteristic established by internal and external analogies: within the aggregates of internal and external conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one employs as an analogy the birth and death universally known in the world.
Re-establishing the coarse impermanence as a metaphor for subtle impermanence is called "of its own kind.

Reiterating the analogy of gross phenomena—such as prosperity and decline—to illustrate subtle impermanence:
the fourth is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to that very [nature] up to what is called the "perfected nature";

Because [the opponent's arguments] are unestablished when stated in terms of the reason (*hetu*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),

Excluding the contradictory certainty (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*):
first, regarding the characteristic of being obtainable as something other than this within the same class (*sapakṣa*),
this [reason] occurs in one part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and occurs pervasively in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

For example, when it is stated: "Sound is not produced by an effort that is uninterrupted [by its result], because it lacks the nature of being impermanent due to [the reason] 'not being produced by an effort that is uninterrupted,'" the thesis—"not being produced by an effort that is uninterrupted"—takes lightning and space as its similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
The probans of impermanence exists in lightning but is absent in space;
taking jars and the like as the heterogeneous instances (*vipakṣa*),
the probans of impermanence is present throughout them.
In this present passage,
it is explained only that [the reason] occurs in one part of the similar instances (sapakṣa); therefore, it says, "this other similar class is obtainable."
Within the similar class (*sapakṣa*) outside of this [subject] itself, this probans of impermanence can be found;
therefore, it is called "this other" (*tad-anyat*).
Second, regarding the characteristic of being found as something other than this in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*):
This refers to a reason that occurs in one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) while occurring pervasively in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
For example, the statement: "Sound is produced by immediate effort because it possesses the nature of impermanence.
In this thesis, jars and the like constitute the similar class.
The reason of impermanence pervades that [subject];
taking lightning and space as the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa),
that reason of impermanence exists in the case of lightning.
In emptiness, there is simply nothing.
Outside of this school, a portion of heterogeneous instances (vipakṣa) can possess the property of impermanence;
therefore, it is said that "this other dissimilar class is obtainable."
Briefly stated, it does not say "pervasive presence in similar instances.
Third, the characteristic of being obtainable in all similar classes constitutes the "common inconclusive" (sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika) reason.
As it is said: "Sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of being an object of cognition.
This reason exists in both the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
In this present passage, we shall first clarify its presence in the similar class.
Fourth, regarding the characteristic of being perceivable by all different classes [of beings],
this constitutes a non-common [reason].
For example, it is said that "sound is eternal because it is audible."
There is no similar instance (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta),
but there is only a dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta). Since nothing other than sound is non-audible,
it is said that "all things of a different class are obtainable."
Fifth, that which is obtained through a dissimilar analogy (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) is a partial application to both sides [of the thesis and its opposite],
such as when one says, "Sound is eternal because it lacks material resistance," and so forth.
Because it occurs in one part of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and also occurs in one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*),
it is called the characteristic obtained through a heterogeneous example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Sixth is the characteristic that is not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
When the constituent causes are incomplete,
it is called "not perfectly accomplished.
Seventh is the characteristic of a teaching that is not well-purified.
For example, in the argument "Sound is eternal because it is produced," this reason exists only in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*);
therefore, the formal proof (*sādhana*) is not well-purified.
The names have been listed above;
in the following explanation, the third point is addressed first.
It says: "If all phenomena are of a nature cognizable by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), this is called the 'characteristic of the obtainability of all similar types.'"
For example, it is like establishing that sound is permanent because it is cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If that were so, the mental consciousness would cognize all phenomena.
Would sound then be permanent simply because it is cognized by the mental consciousness, just as space is?
It is like the case of a jar and so forth: because it is cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), sound is impermanent.

As for the statement: "If all dharmas—whether their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), activity (*karman*), factors (*dharma*), causes (*hetu*), results (*phala*), or distinct marks (*viśeṣa*)—are such that they are called 'the characteristic of all distinct categories being obtainable'..."
This explains the fifth type: partial occurrence within the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

This cause of non-obstruction exists in space but is absent in atoms; jars,
pleasure, and so forth serve as the heterogeneous instances (vipakṣa).
This cause of non-obstruction exists in relation to pleasure and the like, but does not exist in relation to jars and the like; therefore,
it is said that [the relationship] proceeds according to such reciprocal similarities and differences among partial aspects.
