Master Tai said:
In the first case, the reason (*hetu*) established is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For example, if one establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*) that "the aggregate as a whole (*piṇḍa-skandha*) is impermanent," and states the reason:
"because it is cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)."
However, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are likewise cognizable by the mind and are not impermanent, this constitutes the second alternative.
This is as when a thesis is established, such as: "Sound is impermanent."
The reason given is that it is "heard by the ear-consciousness.
However, distinct categories of phenomena such as visible forms and odors are not heard by the ear-consciousness;
nevertheless, they are impermanent.
The reason established is unproven.
If one establishes the thesis that "sound is permanent," yet offers the reason "because it is produced from causes," [the reason is invalid].
However, there is nothing else of a different category that arises from non-appropriating causes;
since such things are impermanent, no such distinct category can be found.
Bei (Bei-shou) said:
First, the third characteristic is explained;
second, the fourth characteristic is explained,
which is the "common indeterminate" (sādhāraṇānaikāntika).
The first definition is explained in three ways:
because it occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (sapakṣa) while occurring pervasively in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa),
it is not determinative regarding the thesis to be established (sādhya).
This is called "non-perfect.
Fourth, the explanation of the second characteristic:
it is because [the reason] occurs in a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) and occurs pervasively in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
The thesis to be established is likewise not determinate:
the fifth [member] explains the sixth characteristic,
and the sixth explains the fifth and seventh characteristics.
Because they are induced by heterogeneous factors in their respective order,
they are not true teachings;
their essential nature is entirely impure.
Jingyun: Among these seven characteristics,
the first four lines subsume the five indeterminate [factors].

That is to say, the first phrase subsumes that which occurs in a portion of the similar class (*sapakṣa*), occurs universally in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), and occurs in a portion of both classes.
The second phrase...
The third phrase— “pervading the similar instances while occurring in only a portion of the dissimilar instances”—
subsumes the common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*).
The fourth phrase subsumes the uncommon indeterminate [factors].
As for the characteristics obtained through the analogies of different classes in the fifth [phrase]:
This contradicts the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the inclusion of phenomena.
Regarding the sixth point, that which is not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
it fails to include four [categories].
The seventh, the characteristic of perfectly pure verbal instruction,
subsumes all other remaining faults.
Fourth is the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*).
Regarding the statement that the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is called the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*):
it refers to the fact that earth is eternally solid by nature, and so forth, up to wind being eternally mobile by nature;
and that good brings about pleasant retribution while evil brings about bitter fruit.
Therefore, it is said that whether a Buddha exists or not, the *dharmatā* remains established and the *dharmadhātu* remains established.
Within the analysis of the aspects (*ākāra*), the seventh [topic] has already been explained.
Next, the eighth—both in its general and specific aspects—is to be explained.
This means that there is one sentence which provides a general heading,
followed by subsequent sentences that explain it in detail and clarify it;
thus, its meaning can be understood.
The general explanation of the fourth category of characteristics within the eleven characteristics of the *Mātṛkā* is hereby concluded.
Next, the fifth characteristic, the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), is explained;
that is to say, what I have described up to this point is termed the characteristic of intrinsic nature.
In the *Mātṛkā*, it is stated that there are "possessing activity" (*sapravṛtti*) and "possessing objects" (*sālambana*),
which explains the essential characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth.
The sixth [section] explains their characteristics as results (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).
This refers to the abandonment of all mundane and supramundane afflictions (*kleśa*).
Mundane paths suppress and abandon afflictions,
while supramundane paths permanently eradicate them.
This explains the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*) and the mundane and supramundane fruits and qualities it induces;
this is the quality of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*).
Seventh, regarding his reception of the instruction:
"characteristic" refers to the fact that when the instruction is proclaimed and revealed to him,
he receives with the wisdom of liberation the qualities of the knowledge and abandonment attained.
He proclaims it for others.
Eighth, the characteristics of those obstructive factors can be known.
9. Regarding those phenomena that accord with the Dharma (*anulomika-dharma-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to one who performs much of what is to be done regarding those phenomena;
that is, one who practices the phenomena that accord with *nirvāṇa* and accomplishes much of what is to be done.
That is called "conformity.
Tenth, regarding the characteristic of their defects:
the aforementioned obstructive dharmas can act as defects.
Eleventh is the characteristic of its excellence,
which refers to all the virtues inherent in the aforementioned factors conducive to awakening.
Sixth is the clarification of the meaning of the uncommon dhāraṇīs.
Within this, there is first the request and subsequently the response.
In the response, there is both prose and verse.
Within the prose, there is first the command to listen and the permission to speak.
Next follows the formal explanation;
the third section is a brief conclusion.
Within the formal explanation, there are three statements.
The initial statement that "all phenomena of affliction and purity are devoid of activity," etc.,
serves to refute the Vaiseṣikas and others who posit a real activity (*kāritra*), as well as those who,
while asserting a real nature (*svabhāva*), maintain the existence of a real self (*ātman*) rather than a merely conventional function.
Furthermore, regarding those who repeatedly resort to such provisional designations:
within the Buddha’s Dharma, beginners first cling to the existence of suffering, its origin, and defilement as being predetermined,
and they subsequently grasp at cessation and the path as things to be attained later.
Just as with that conceptual construction,
since this thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is ultimately without substance, how could there be any sequence of before or after? However,
if one considers the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) in terms of its causes and conditions regarding defilement and purity:
It is not that there is no sequence of prior and subsequent.

The subsequent statement, "from ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and heterodox beings (*visabhāga-jana*) up to those engaged in wrong application," means that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of these heterodox beings are accompanied by afflictions (*kleśa*) and are not pliant (*akarmaṇya*).
It is called the "body of coarse heaviness" (*dausthulyakāya*).
Within this body of coarse heaviness, one clings to the intrinsic nature and specific distinctions of persons and phenomena.

Due to the conditions of the seeds of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) from past habitual practice and false views, one conceives of a self and what belongs to the self, thinking, "I can see, hear, and so forth."
If there are those who have already descended according to reality,
next it is explained that if one knows false conceptualization,
one is then able to forever sever the body of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Regarding the phrase "attaining the non-abiding of all afflictions" and so forth:
nirvāṇa is termed the non-abiding of afflictions.
There are three verses on this point in the *kārikā*.
The preceding prose commentary correctly explains the three phrases of the verse in their respective order.
The seventh section clarifies the characteristics of the arising of the body and mind of enjoyment;
it consists of two questions and answers.
The first question and answer provide a general explanation of the arising of the Buddha-mind;
the subsequent question and answer explain that although the Buddhas lack formal application (*prayoga*),
their minds nevertheless arise due to the power of the application of internal means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*).
There are the elements of the thesis, the example, and the application.
The eighth [section] clarifies the meaning of the transformative mind having both a mind and no-mind;
the mind itself cannot be transformed.
Therefore, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Buddha has no mind that relies upon itself;
rather, it benefits sentient beings in response to conditions by relying on the mind of the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya).
Therefore, it is said that there is a mind dependent on others.
The ninth [section] clarifies the two distinct characteristics of the Tathāgata’s practice and the Tathāgata’s realm;
herein, this refers to taking the pure lands of all Buddhas as the object of cognition.
It is called "the conduct of the Tathāgata.
Based on the activity of benefiting sentient beings through the five immeasurable objects as its conditions,
it is called "the sphere of the Tathāgata."

The tenth section clarifies that among the eight aspects [of a Buddha], the three—attaining perfect enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering great parinirvāṇa—are all devoid of dualistic characteristics.
This means that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is free from these three marks.
To undergo transformation in response to conditions is called ultimate purity;
the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Tathāgata likewise undergoes transformation in response to conditions.
Because they are constantly manifested,
these three characteristics exist.
The eleventh [point] clarifies that the Buddha’s transformative virtue gives rise to merit in others from afar.

Question: Since sentient beings are unable to see, hear of, or serve the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and his body of self-enjoyment, what is the causal condition for [the Buddha] with respect to all sentient beings?
Answer: Zhongjing says:
The Tathāgata is the causal condition for that [transformation body] as its predominant object of focus;
therefore, it generates great merit for others.
Furthermore, that transformation body is sustained by the power of the Tathāgata.
The enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) produces merit for others in the near term by arising within their own bodies,
while the dharma body (dharmakāya) sustains the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) in the distant term;
thus, both of these two bodies also generate merit for others.
Tài says:
"The Tathāgata is the wisdom of the saṃbhogakāya (enjoyment body).
It is by virtue of this wisdom [that he is so called]."
They transform into forms and sounds;
because the forms and sounds of the Tathāgata serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings give rise to appearances that resemble the forms and sounds of the Tathāgata.
It is precisely the form and sound of the Tathāgata as an object of perception; however,
this is merely an indirect object of perception (adhipatālambana),
not a direct object of perception (pratyakṣālambana).
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is the causal condition for that predominant object of focus,
because it is capable of directly manifesting as form and sound.
Twelfth, this clarifies the distinction between the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata and the bodies of liberation of the two vehicles.
Jingbei and others state:
"As for the statement that the Tathāgata’s dharma-body, for the sake of all sentient beings, [manifests] the light of great wisdom and the images of innumerable transformation bodies,
this is spoken in reference to superior and remote conditions."
When emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth emerge from the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*),
they constitute a direct dependent origination (*pratyaya*).
As for the statement that "they are sustained by sentient beings of great majestic power," it means:
By the power sustained by the Sun and Moon Devas, they emit great radiance;
this serves as an analogy for how the Dharma-body realized by the Buddhas of Great Majestic Virtue is able to manifest the reflected images of their transformation-bodies (nirmāṇakāya).
"By the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings" refers to the second condition;
it is due to the predominant power of the karma for cultivating light performed by sentient beings within darkness.
Just as that crystal gem emits great light when stimulated by the sun and moon,
it is analogous to how sentient beings possess the karmic conditions for seeing the Buddha.
That Dharmakāya emits a great radiance;
it is not like other things such as water, fire, or crystal gems that can emit light.
This is analogous to the liberation-body (vimuktikāya) realized by those of the two vehicles.
This is because the first two functions are absent.

The thirteenth [chapter] clarifies that through the majestic power and sustaining presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whether in terms of the Path or its practice, all sentient beings within the three realms now possess perfection of body and wealth.
The "path" refers to the ten wholesome courses of action;
the "practice" refers to the sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind, and so forth.
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands this path and this practice.
This body is the cause for wealth;
how could one who practices this path in accordance with the teachings not speak of it?
In all places, one attains the perfection of both body and wealth;
according to this principle,
it is called "abiding in majestic power."
Question: It may be so for the realms of desire and form;
but how can there be wealth and treasures in the formless realm?
The commentary explains:
Within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), that which is properly termed "name" (*nāma*) refers to the body;
that which is transformed by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is termed "wealth" (*bhoga*).
Furthermore, it is explained that while the body pervades the three realms,
wealth exists only in the desire and form realms.
These are collectively termed the bodies and wealth of the three realms.
The fourteenth [section] clarifies that in the defiled land, eight matters are easily obtained and two matters are difficult to obtain.
In the Pure Land,
these two matters are easily obtained,
while those eight matters are difficult to obtain.
This can be understood according to the text.
The benefit of establishing the name at the time [of its application] below may be known.
In the seventy-ninth fascicle, the first section on the *yogasthāna* of initial retention (*ādhiṣṭhāna-yoga*) has been concluded.
From here below begins the second section, the determination of the *yogasthāna* of retention according to the Dharma (*anudharma-yoga*).
This section consists of four chapters.
In this [work], only the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (Decisive Compendium) is established;
the first three [sections] are not subject to such analysis because they are easily understood.
The Master Ki and others state:
"This first chapter further provides a definitive resolution regarding the meaning of the five immeasurables within the 'Chapter on Merits' (Guṇavarga).
From the section 'Based upon the four kinds of abidings' onwards..."
This indeed refers to the *yoga* that follows the Dharma with certainty;
although there is this explanation,
we now rely on Master Jing.
The judgment is as previously stated.
Within this, the initial restatement of what has already been established is concluded;
next follows the formal determination.
The textual divisions consist of nine parts.
The first clarifies the distinctions among worlds.
Jing says:
It is said that in the world of purity there are no hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts, nor is there the triple world, nor is there any experience of suffering;
it does not say, however, that there are no humans or devas.
Thus, it is permitted that there are bodhisattvas in the Pure Land who take the form of humans or devas, yet they are not bound by the three realms.
Those bodhisattvas who have already entered the third stage and take birth there do so through the power of their vows.
Regarding the statement that those from the first bhūmi upward all attain rebirth therein, as for why it specifies the third bhūmi:

this is said in terms of characteristics; it is because one attains meditative concentration in the third bhūmi, and by relying on that concentration to cultivate contemplation, one then attains rebirth. Thus, this explanation is made.
There are neither ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) nor those who are not ordinary beings; nor are there those of the two vehicles.
If bodhisattvas who are ordinary beings were to be born there, this would be discussed in terms of the pure land of actual retribution (*vipākabhūmi*).
The following applies generally across various scriptures.

Question: If there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), bodhisattvas, or those of the two vehicles who are not ordinary beings who can be born there, for what reason does the Bodhisattva teaching state that bodhisattvas and others, through their vows and aspirations, shall all be reborn there?
Answer: It was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) in order to transform indolent sentient beings and cause them to accumulate roots of goodness.
Tai says: "To speak according to the actual principle..."
Bodhisattvas of the first and second stages can also be born there;
however, this present account refers to those Bodhisattvas from the third stage upward who are free from desire and are born in that Pure Land.
It is only said that those of the third stage are born in the Pure Land;
there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or noble ones of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) who are ordinary bodhisattvas who can be born there.
If those of the two vehicles abide in tranquility, they immediately enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
If one has generated the bodhicitta, those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) immediately belong to the category of bodhisattvas;
therefore, the noble beings of the two vehicles who abide in tranquility never again arise [in saṃsāra],
and ordinary bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) likewise never again arise [in saṃsāra].
The following explains the intent of the sutra.
Elsewhere it is said that if bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles wish to be born there, they shall all be reborn there;
this was spoken by the Tathāgata with a "different-time" intention (*kālavipākābhiprāya*).
Jizang says:

This passage is precisely as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* regarding the Pure Land, where there are no ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), exactly as the text describes.
Since ancient times, Paramārtha and others have maintained that the realization of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and above involves the severing of the grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-grāha*).
They are called "noble ones" (*ārya*).
This meaning is not so;
according to this treatise and others, they are called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).
Nor has he yet abandoned the afflictions.
If there were no ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) below [this level],
then the following questions and answers would be raised, citing scriptures as the basis for inquiry.
The Sūtra states that one may attain birth in that land by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times; why, then,
is it said here that one attains birth only at the third stage?
Answer:
The meaning of the text clarifies that it was spoken with the intention of referring to a different time;
therefore, it says one is born in the Pure Land, yet ordinary beings cannot be born there immediately.

Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and other treatises all judge that the various sūtras stating that ordinary beings are born in the Pure Land are spoken with the intention of referring to a different time;
they do not mean that birth occurs immediately.
Regarding its pure lands, there are three kinds:
first, the land of self-enjoyment;
second, the land for others.
This refers to the Land of Immeasurable Life and others.
Third is the transformation-pure land of attachment,
which refers to the temporary manifestation of pure characteristics within a defiled land.
As stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, [the Buddha] pressed the earth with his toe to manifest the characteristics of the Pure Land.
From ancient times, many virtuous masters have raised debates on this matter;
some have said that the transformed manifestation of the Pure Land has a separate location.
Regarding the nine grades of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
some say there are no distinct locations for them,
just as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* describes how the ground transforms when pressed by the foot.
Furthermore, as the *Mahāyāna-samaya-sūtra* states:
"Attaining enlightenment in a defiled land is called the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body)," and so forth.
Such are these two interpretations.
One may freely choose and reject [the options].
Second, it clarifies how a bodhisattva, by relying on the four abodes, can accomplish four matters.
Jing says:
Among the four abidings, the abiding of joy, the abiding of morality, and the abiding of mind correspond to the first three stages.
The abiding of wisdom corresponds to the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages.
The attainment of the factors of enlightenment occurs in the fourth stage.
The truths consist of five stages;
dependent origination consists of six stages;
and the skillful knowledge that establishes the unique qualities—which transcends the knowledge commonly realized by the two vehicles—is as follows:
The fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are identical to those of the two vehicles;
from the seventh stage upward, one transcends them.
Therefore, it is said that one transcends the wisdom commonly realized by the two vehicles.
Within this context, the wisdom that establishes the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) extends up to the wisdom that establishes the truths (*satya-vyavasthāpana-jñāna*).
From the seventh ground upward, there is the wisdom that universally contemplates both the conventional establishment (*vyavasthāna*) and the non-establishment (*avyavasthāna*) of the two truths.
Among these, "shared wisdom" refers to the wisdom of realization attained by relying on dependent origination.
Although it is referred to simply as "dependent origination" based on its ultimate point of reference,
the wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) on the fourth stage and the wisdom of the four truths (catuḥsatya) on the fifth stage are both included within this shared wisdom.
This distinguishes the common realized wisdom that has been transcended.
One practices generosity based on the first stage (bhūmi) and maintains ethical discipline on the second stage.
Through precepts one attains one's own person;
through giving one attains wealth and treasures.
Therefore, it is said that they increase and excel more and more.
Regarding those who, for the benefit of sentient beings, turn back from the various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and are reborn in the desire realm through the power of their great vows:
they do so by taking karma belonging to the desire realm as the cause and their vows and meditative absorptions as the conditions.
He is reborn in the desire realm.
T'ai says:
"In the second stage of abiding."
It is called "perfect" because it possesses the nature of śīla that is free from all transgressions;
this śīla is free from all stinginess.
Therefore, it is called the perfection of relinquishment.
Furthermore, another interpretation is that through this precept, one is able to abandon both stinginess and the violation of the precepts.
Therefore, it is called "renunciation through ethical discipline.
Third, the bodhisattva’s mental attention (*manasikāra*) regarding suffering and pleasure, as well as their abiding, is explained;
the wisdom of suchness (*yathāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*) is termed mental attention.
The wisdom of suchness is called "abiding.
Fourth, the four superior grades of hindrances and the methods for removing these hindrances are clarified.
If the four superior grades of hindrances arise prior to the stages (bhūmi),
and one fails to purify them, one will not enter the stages; that is,
one does not enter the fundamental stages.
Regarding the gradual progression through the stages (*bhūmi*):
this refers to the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) of the stages.
Alternatively, it is explained as follows.
The first stage is called the Bodhisattva Stage;
from the second stage upward, they are called the successive stages.
First, regarding those who commit offenses through defilement:
This constitutes a violation of a minor precept.
Second, it is to disparage the Mahāyāna teachings;
this is one of the four grave offenses.
Third, those who have not yet accumulated roots of virtue;
their practices prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are not yet perfected.
Fourth, those who possess a mind of defiled attachment.
Before the stages (*bhūmi*), one cultivates wholesome deeds while craving defiled fruits.
The following clarifies four methods for purifying and eliminating obstacles,
which respectively remove the four preceding obstacles.
The fifth clarifies how Bodhisattvas on the Great Grounds (mahābhūmi) eliminate four kinds of subtle secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The first is attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*),
which is the attachment within the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Those who cling to the teachings develop attachment toward them; thus,
although the coarse [afflictions] have been severed,
the subtle ones still persist.
This refers to the obstacles of the fourth stage.
Second is the mental orientation of the two vehicles,
which consists of revulsion toward birth and death and a longing for parinirvāṇa.
This refers to the obstacle of the fifth stage.
Third is attachment to meditative absorption (*samāpatti*),
which arises within the third stage.
It obstructs the fourth stage;
it consists of the activities of the four classes of Māras,
such as the mind’s scattering toward worldly affairs and their objects of perception.
These hinder the cultivation of contemplative practice and are all the deeds of Māra.
Question:

The text above states that one must first understand all the afflictions possessed by Bodhisattvas on the higher stages before they can give rise to their own cultivation of merit and the benefiting of others;
how then can these words be easily understood in their full extent?
The commentary explains:
The previous [statement] was based on coarse afflictions, which must be known before they arise;
the present [statement] is based on subtle afflictions, which are difficult to know universally.
Furthermore, since the previous [passage] was based on the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) while the present one is based on the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),
there is no contradiction.
The sixth [section] explains the characteristics of the eleven stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the Bodhisattva of the first stage who transcends fear and attains the unsurpassed Dharma:
this is because they transcend the five fears and attain the noble Dharma.
Regarding the Bodhisattva of the second stage who naturally obtains [the qualities] within the context of self-discipline: [this is because...]
Subduing is the natural law of this precept, whereby one attains freedom from transgressions and the like;
it brings to rest all that is studied by those of the two vehicles,
and the essence of the precepts it upholds surpasses the conduct of the precepts studied by those two vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "thereby realizing the light of *jñeya*":
*jñeya* here refers to that which is to be known.
Through the power of this meditative concentration, one brings forth the light of wisdom regarding the objects of knowledge.
By means of this, one who is skilled in establishing all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) exactly as they have been realized,
personally accomplishes the path-factors and establishes the teaching for others.
The fifth stage surpasses the mundane wisdom of the preceding three stages.
Furthermore, it surpasses the wisdom regarding the factors of the path of the two vehicles of the fourth stage.
In the sixth stage, one dwells with a sense of revulsion toward the formations of dependent origination.
Regarding those who dwell frequently in and incline toward mental attention directed at the signless realm:
although Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage take both the ultimate and conventional as their objects,
they predominantly enter into the signless.
Regarding "attaining mastery over all marks on the eighth stage," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"In accordance with whatever marks one seeks."
Mastery over will,
and mastery over names and signs;
furthermore, there is the traditional interpretation.
On the eighth stage, one is able to know that the internal body and the external vessel-world are composed of a certain number of atoms, and all these can be made to accord with one's will;
this is called mastery over names and signs (*nāmanimitta-vaśitā*). As for "mastery": [it refers to...]
He manifests various lands directly for the sake of sentient beings.
The "mastery of meditative concentration" (samādhi-vaśitā) encompasses the preceding two [mastery of lifespan and mastery of mind].
Furthermore, by relying on meditative concentration, one gives rise to all meritorious qualities and attains mastery over them.
This is called mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā*).
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"In the eighth stage, the Bodhisattva eliminates ignorance regarding the objects of form (*rūpa-dhātu*)," and so forth.
Mastery over names and signs:
that which attains mastery over names, phrases, and syllables in the ninth stage is the unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, "attaining faultlessness" means that regarding the meaning [of phenomena],
there is unimpeded knowledge,
yet one does not become attached to that meaning.
Therefore it is called "blameless.
That which is immeasurable and vast is the unimpeded sacrifice.
Because one knows all speech and wisdom throughout the ten directions,
it is called "vast. Furthermore,
because one has attained vast and unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), one is able to gladden the minds of all sentient beings.
The unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition.
Having attained that which is shared by all Tathāgatas upon the tenth stage—
formerly known as "consecration" (abhiṣeka)— it is here called "sprinkling."
Just as when the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch assumes his father’s office,
the waters of the four oceans are taken to prepare fragrant bathwater with which he is sprinkled upon the crown of his head;
he is then named an anointed Kṣatriya Great King.
The same applies to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Once the training and practice are perfected,
the Buddhas of the ten directions emit light from the crown of their heads (*uṣṇīṣa*).
They all enter his crown,
whereby he receives the office of Buddha-wisdom;
even when the various Buddhas emit light from beneath their feet, it all enters his feet.
Therefore, when it is said that one has already attained the same sprinkling as the Tathāgata and has already attained the great Dharma-body like a cloud,
this refers to the *tathatā*-dharma-body and the fivefold dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).
Because they can cover and extinguish the coarse body of birth and death— which is like space—
and because they have already attained all great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are also called Tathāgatas;
for although those of the tenth stage are not yet Buddhas, [they possess these qualities].
Having attained great supernormal powers and abiding in the stage of Equal Enlightenment,
their coarse attributes are identical to those of a Buddha,
and they are also titled Tathāgata.
One enters the eleventh stage,
which is named "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue).
The seventh [section] clarifies the fulfillment of the outflowing results attained through the cultivation of the various stages.
Regarding the statement that "one who dwells on the stage of practice through resolute belief relies upon the ten stages to cultivate the ten types of practice":
this refers to one who dwells prior to the [ten] stages and looks up to the ten types of dharma-practice of the ten stages as their object of study.
That is to say, writing, upholding, and so forth are called "cultivation.
Alternatively, one may aspire to study the ten dharma-practices of the ten perfections cultivated on the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is explained that one may aspire to study the ten practices beginning with faith.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, when one realizes the pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*), at that moment one suddenly attains all the stages (*bhūmi*)," Jingbei explains in the same way:
"The seeds of all the stages are entirely inherent from the beginning."
When attaining the first stage (bhūmi),
the seeds of all stages are simultaneously perfumed and activated, causing them all to increase;
this is called "attaining the first stage instantaneously."
Another interpretation is that,
although the practices of the ten stages are not yet perfected when one first aspires to cultivate them in the first stage,
one nonetheless partially attains the ten stages.
This is called "attaining all at once.
The various masters of the Western Regions differ in their interpretations.
One interpretation is as follows:
According to this text,
the merits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the Buddha stage (*buddhabhūmi*) are each distinct and different;
therefore, the seeds capable of producing them are likewise different.
Regarding the statement that "in this context, all stages are attained instantaneously at the first stage," this is spoken in reference to the *dharmatā-bīja* (innate seeds).
According to principle, these *dharmatā-bījas* have existed from time immemorial and are not something newly acquired at this point.
As for the term "attainment" (prāpti),
it is so called because it functions to induce the arising of the fruit;
therefore, it is named "attainment."
There are three kinds of attainment (*prāpti*).
Here, it is designated as "attainment" with reference to seeds (*bīja*) and mastery (*vaśitā*).
First interpretation:
Because one is able to obtain the seeds of all stages,
it is called "attaining all at once" (sudden attainment).
It does not mean that the seeds of the qualities of the various stages (*bhūmi*) have distinct names;
therefore, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*).
As for "natural outflow" (*niṣyanda*), it refers to all the majestic powers (*vibhūti*) present within all the stages subsequent to having realized [the path].
Master Jingbei said:
"The fulfillment of the mind in each stage (*bhūmi*) is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for entering and abiding [in that stage].
Furthermore, the fulfillment of the mind in a preceding stage looks upward to and studies the various paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) of the subsequent stages."
This refers to the mental continuum (*cittasaṃtāna*) of the stage being filled.
Xuanzang states:
"In all ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), this applies to both the phases of entry (*praveśa*) and abiding (*sthiti*)."
It is called "attainment" (prāpti).
The stage of the fulfillment of the fruit of the grounds is called "after attainment."
As stated in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages):
"All the paths of preparation— including supernormal powers, majestic virtue, the stages of setting out, and the fruits—
are the attainment of the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) during the two phases of entering and abiding."
Regarding the fulfillment of the stages:
within each individual stage, one passes through many great eons and is able to spontaneously realize all the virtues of the stages as they are extolled in the various sūtras.
This is the characteristic of fulfillment.
The eighth [section] clarifies the distinction between the realization of the dharma-realm by śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
Jing says:
Regarding the statement that there are five types of entry into the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*):
among the śrāvakas, there are three.
The first is those who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).
One enters the path of seeing because one has doubly abandoned desire and reached its exhaustion.
One enters the path of seeing because of these two reasons.
Third, those who have detached from the desires of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness,
and who enter the path of seeing—
namely, the solitary realizers (pratyekabuddhas) and bodhisattvas— are called the five types of persons.
Question:
As with the śrāvakas, there are three types of entry into the state of noble ones,
namely those who are bound by all fetters and so forth.
It is not yet known whether Pratyekabuddhas also have the three types of persons—such as those still bound by all fetters—and whether they enter the noble state in the same manner as Śrāvakas.
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
"As for those who are like the rhinoceros horn..."
Those who have subdued all afflictions from the level of the sphere of nothingness downward,
and who enter into right determination based on the fourth dhyāna to realize the latter two fruits, are the group-practitioners (gaṇacārin).
He is the same as those śrāvakas.
Ji (Baoshan Zhiyi) further states:
"The five types refer to the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva."
Among them, one who has attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna) is a person of gradual progression;
all others are those who transcend.
Herein, these five types of persons are collectively categorized into two.
That is to say, the former four are for śrāvakas,
while those for bodhisattvas are for bodhisattvas;
thus, there are two kinds.
Regarding the term "the characteristic of permanence," this refers to the dharmatā that is primordially unborn and inexhaustible;
it is precisely suchness as manifested by the emptiness of persons.
If its essence were permanent,
it would be without arising and without exhaustion;
such would be its characteristic of quiescence.

That which is called the "dharma-nature of the dissociation from the suffering of afflictions" refers to the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) that is the dissociation from the obstacles of delusion, the afflictions, and suffering.
The followers of the two vehicles, while in the stage of preparatory means, seek that which is eternally abiding, quiescent, and unconditioned.
They manifest the appearance of nirvana because they seek later realization of true suchness; thus,
they swiftly proceed toward extinction.

Regarding the fact that the self-characteristic is precisely the lack of self-nature (anātmatā) in the true dharma—the suchness of conceptual differentiation—wherein the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is not established as a real entity:
while the bodhisattva is engaged in skillful means, [he realizes this].

However, when the mind investigates the five sets of five factors such as characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, they are found to be empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and non-existent according to verbal designations.
Through this, one enters into the true nature (*tathatā*) of self-characteristics,
wherein there is ultimately nothing to be sought or realized.
Because their intention is to abide eternally in the tranquility of nirvāṇa,
they do not swiftly seek their own extinction. Therefore,
it is said that herein the śrāvakas, through the characteristic of distinction, penetrate the dharmadhātu and enter the state of right nature beyond birth.
Regarding "due to the absence of the notion of passing away":
this refers to giving rise to the notion of permanence and the notion of security with respect to nirvāṇa.
They conceive the notion of tranquility regarding nirvāṇa,
and thus give rise to the notion of revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Alternatively, there are those such as śrāvakas who, having heard the Dharma taught by others concerning the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), partially dedicate themselves toward awakening (*bodhi*).
This refers to those of indeterminate lineage (aniyata-gotra).
A certain portion of the śrāvakas who are solely intent upon tranquility (śamaikāyana) can only enter [the path] with extreme difficulty and do not apply themselves with diligence.
Tái says:
Śrāvakas realize the suchness manifested by the absence of "mine" in persons; however,
they have not realized the essential nature of suchness itself,
but only the characteristic of the specific absence of self within that suchness.
Therefore, it is called the "distinguished characteristic" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Because the Bodhisattva realizes the self-nature of *tathatā* as manifested by the dharma’s lack of "mine-ness," it is called the "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
As for those śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage,
they may, through the influence of others— namely, when various buddhas proclaim the teaching for them—
hear it and subsequently dedicate themselves toward bodhi before finally attaining realization.
Because they have long believed in the non-self of persons,
it is extremely difficult for them to enter the non-self of phenomena.
Among those śrāvakas who incline toward tranquility, there are also two types.
Although one portion hears the teaching that all phenomena are without self,
they do not believe it at all and are unable to penetrate it;
another portion has slight faith and slight realization.
Having failed to enter [the path] despite extreme hardship, he diligently practiced for unsurpassed bodhi.
Bei said:
"There are two kinds of śrāvakas."
First, there are śrāvakas who are not deluded regarding the Dharma;
having heard the teaching on specific characteristics,
they turn away from the Lesser Vehicle and direct themselves toward the Great Vehicle, practicing with diligent effort.
Second, the foolish śrāvakas,
although they have realized self-characteristics, do not apply themselves with diligence.
The ninth clarifies the purity of the wheel of the three periods of time.
That is to say: having no longing for the past,
no expectation for the future,
and no attachment to the present.
It is said that being without attachment to the three periods of time and so forth is called the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*).
Thus far, the first two sections of the sequential determination of the three supports have been completed.
Hereafter follows the third: the determination of the *dhāraṇī* of the ultimate stage of yoga (*yogasthāna*).
In this [treatise], there are five chapters; however,
only the "Chapter on Establishing the Decisive" (決建立品) is explicitly set forth here,
because the preceding four are already evident.
It is not a definitive analysis.
Within this, first two questions and answers are presented.
What are these two questions?
First is the question concerning establishment;
second is the question concerning inclusion.
In the response, the establishment is first analyzed to answer the former question.
The subsequent section clarifies the mutual inclusion [of these qualities] in order to answer the latter question.
Within this, there is first an explanation followed by a conclusion.
Although the explanation contains eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they are combined into nine sections.
First, it clarifies that his physical conduct is without fault;
second, it clarifies that his verbal conduct is without fault;
third, it clarifies that his mental conduct is without fault.
Fourth, he is clearly aware and free from divergent thoughts; fifth, his mind is never unsettled;
sixth, he possesses no equanimity that is not preceded by discernment.
Seventh, the explanation of the non-declinings:
first, desire; second, vigor; third, mindfulness; fourth, concentration; fifth, wisdom; sixth, liberation; and seventh, the knowledge and vision of liberation.
As for why they are called "seven kinds": [it is because...]
Within the sixth liberation, two types are distinguished;
thus, there are seven.
The eighth clarifies that the three karmas follow the movement of wisdom.
In the case of the Tathāgata, the three types of action (trikarma) have wisdom as their preceding path; this refers to the causal origination (*samutthāna*).
Wisdom that follows along refers to the momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*);
therefore, there is no indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) [action].
The ninth section clarifies the three types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
The following section distinguishes their mutual inclusion in order to answer the subsequent question.
It states: "In this context, the first four are the qualities of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*)."
The three types of action are without error,
and there is no divergent thought;
this constitutes the quality of being free from forgetfulness as well as the eradication of habitual tendencies.
The next one is that which is subsumed by great compassion;
this refers to the great compassion of a mind that is never not in meditative concentration.
It should be understood that the remaining thirteen are subsumed by the sublime knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Furthermore, as for the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) mentioned in other sūtras, they are displayed there for the sake of inspiring pure faith in those to be converted; however, they are not established as primary marks (lakṣaṇa), because the secondary marks manifest as subtle features.
Therefore, it is not established that there is a characteristic of being "good.
As for the establishment of various characteristics, it can be understood as already extensively demonstrated in the "Chapter on Establishment" (*Pratisthāpana-paṭala*).
Regarding the statement, "One should know that from these secondary marks (anuvyañjana) those various secondary marks are derived," Master Jìngbèi says:
"From the section on the marks (lakṣaṇa) in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the meanings of the various secondary marks in other sūtras are derived."
Master Tai said:

"From this point forward, regarding the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) explained in the 'Chapter on Establishing,' one should know that they are distinguished from the various specific secondary marks described in those other sutras."
The sequential determination of the three *dhāraṇīs* above is now complete.
The following one fascicle of scripture is also an exposition of the text of the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
Regarding this *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*:
Previously, three or four fascicles of this [text] had already been translated here;
they are no longer extant.
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra* in four fascicles explains sixteen kinds of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Students should examine and verify this accordingly.
Within this, first sixteen dharma-gates are listed,
and second, these gates are explained in detail.
The first [section] explains erroneous conduct.
In the middle [of this section], eight types are initially enumerated;
since each preceding one induces the subsequent one, it is said that "each subsequent one is induced."
The second part, the detailed explanation of the eight types, consists of eight sections.
The first explains the provisions for the wisdom of decline;
within this, there is first a general explanation followed by a specific one.
This section has three parts.
First, it clarifies the four kinds of retrogression.
Second, it explains how, due to retrogression, four kinds of dharmas that are contrary to wisdom arise.
Third, the essential characteristics of the four types of retrogression are presented.
Regarding the first point, "not allowing others to hear," this is stated from the perspective of those who have attained mastery and possess power.
Regarding those who create obstacles to hearing the Dharma:
based on the fact that a person lacking power cannot, at that time, prevent others from listening,
they later act as an obstacle to their hearing the Dharma.
Next, the four dharmas that are contrary to the dharma of falling away (parihāṇadharman) are explained.
Within this, first there is a general enumeration and inquiry;
subsequently, these are applied to the four aforementioned dharmas.
This can be understood from the text.
Below, the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the four types of retrogression are presented;
herein, the essential characteristics of these four dharmas are first explained individually.
Regarding the subsequent section on the three types of wisdom used to distinguish retrogression and loss,
the *Zhongjing* (Middle Scripture) states:
"Based on one's own inferior thorough comprehension, understanding, and proclamation, one clings to [the notion of] superior thorough comprehension, understanding, and proclamation," and so forth.

The first phrase refers to one who, relying on their own perverse and erroneous wisdom, understands, explains, and adheres to the verbal teachings they have heard, yet falsely claims to have correctly understood, comprehended, and explained them.
The latter phrase refers to the thorough comprehension, understanding, and proclamation of the dependent nature as wholesome wisdom;
"clinging" refers to the thorough comprehension, understanding, and proclamation of the dependent nature as unwholesome.
Regarding "thorough comprehension, understanding, and proclamation":
Because one understands the Dharma being proclaimed at the time of hearing it.
Next is the explanation of the second [obstacle], the loss of right mindfulness (*smṛti-pramoṣa*).
Master Zhongjingbei said:
One gives rise to confusion regarding four types of persons:
first, regarding the person who points out a fault; and so on, up to the fourth, regarding the virtuous person among fellow practitioners of the holy life, one confuses their own transgressions.
He raises those offenses as separate matters and speaks otherwise to confuse his own faults.
Regarding one who is confused about the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) present before them:
because they do not correctly receive instruction from the teacher, they become confused and thus obstruct the cultivation of the three trainings.
Regarding those who have reached the stage of practicing with the resolve that gives rise to confusion toward the Mahāyāna:
there are some who wish to study the Mahāyāna practice,
yet when they speak to them, [the teacher] says that the three vehicles are not distinct.
To say that there is a distinction between the three vehicles through conceptual discrimination is a grave error.
Regarding those who cause confusion among teachers of the Dharma by exposing their secret points:
toward such persons who possess the qualities of a teacher of the Dharma, [one should maintain a respectful distance].
"He himself does not listen to [the confession],
nor does he cause another to listen to his own offense.
Regarding the latter two points, Master Tai explains:
Regarding those who practice the Mahāyāna and further desire its benefits, as well as those who desire to practice correctly—it is said that these people are "evil" in summary;
thus, it is stated that there is no distinction [between them], while enumerating and distinguishing their various faults.
Thus, one incites confusion regarding the superior resolve and correct practice of others;
because one is personally confused regarding the person who teaches the Dharma,
one exposes that person's hidden and secret faults.
Third, the explanation of the destruction of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).
Master Zhongjing says:
"This refers to those who, competing with others for superior power, give rise to various pure dharmas through the application of effort in improper circumstances."
The matter of inciting strife destroys the pure, white dharmas.
Although it is said that one engages in the preparatory application for the site of the white dharmas, there are three kinds of faults of wrong practice;
this constitutes the second [section] in general.
The specific characteristics (lakṣaṇa) constitute three;
together with the preceding, they become four.
Below, three phrases are opened up, each explaining two conditions.
Regarding the two conditions for defiled attachment: first, improper enjoyment; second, dwelling amidst excessive entanglement.
As for improper enjoyment, it refers to when, upon receiving a gift, one uses material wealth to practice favoritism or distribute merit.
To gather in a great assembly and mutually entice one another is called "dwelling amidst much confusion.
Due to these causes and conditions, although one initiates the application of the white dharmas (pure qualities), because of such improper conduct, there is the fault of defiled attachment.

One should know that there are two conditions for the fault of holding wrong views: first, those who slander and deny the True Dharma; second, those who cling to what is not the True Dharma and take it to be the True Dharma. Thus, even if the former type of person practices giving, because they possess wrong views, [their merit is deficient].
The faults regarding the two conditions arise from the fault of undertaking [the precepts] due to two conditions;
this may be understood from the text.
Master Tái says:
For example, if two people both contend over the creation of a Buddha-offering bowl, it is unreasonable for them to give rise to various pure dharmas and virtues;
therefore, this is called "application in an improper sphere" (asthāna-prayoga).
To enjoy things in an improper manner is called "wrong enjoyment.
To dwell in a state of clamor and bustle is called "being amidst much distraction."

In the fourth section, the explanation of malicious intent, it is said that one should understand the lack of faith and compliance toward the Great Teacher by means of three characteristics: namely, regarding him as having substantial existence, as being venerable and supreme, and as being one who has attained knowledge.
Excellence is virtue;
attainment is capacity.
This refers to the lack of faith and compliance regarding that which possesses substance, virtue, and capacity.
Regarding the phrase "due to two kinds of characteristics and because of delighting in them": first,
by receiving the offerings and respect of sentient beings who possess great wisdom and great merit, one may,
through attachment, fall away from wholesome qualities such as diligent application and so forth.
Second, because they are constantly followed by those who delight in great wisdom and merit,
they fall away from wholesome dharmas.
The fourth point is omitted here without further explanation.
The fifth explains those who are difficult to subdue,
as in the text.
The sixth explains those who practice on non-paths.
This is a transgression of the Way.
First, one does not preach the Dharma to establish faith in those who are already established in faith, thereby failing to further develop their confidence.
Second, when there are people turning from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, [one fails to support them].
Third, when seeing sentient beings of indeterminate nature who have regressed from the Great Vehicle to seek the Lesser Vehicle, one fails to admonish or counsel them,
nor does one praise the virtues of the Mahāyāna or censure the faults of the Hīnayāna.
Fourth, regarding those who take pleasure in the body and abide by the precepts, they praise them;
regarding those who do not abide by the precepts, they censure them.
Yet, due to a mind of favoritism and partisanship, they fail to praise those who should be praised and fail to censure those who should be censured.
This is called the "Discourse on Unevenness.
The seventh [section] explains associating with those who are not virtuous,
as in the text.
The eighth interpretation is that it does not accord with its meaning.
To say "not according with its meaning" rather than "not as its meaning" is merely a redundancy; there is no distinct significance to it.
Furthermore, it may also not be like conventional truth, which is not the reality of suchness (*tathatā*).
The preceding section concludes the first gate, the Gate of Erroneous Practice.
Below, the second gate, the Gate of Correct Practice, is elucidated.
Among these, the first provides a general indication.
It is called "right conduct" because it reverses the eight types of wrong conduct previously mentioned and draws forth eight kinds of practice.
Regarding the phrase "drawing forth detachment":
To distance oneself from the aforementioned faults, the intended antidotes are explained.
By reversing those preceding faults, the subsequent ones are successively induced, thus explaining the eight antidotes.
Furthermore, these eight kinds of successive antidotes are the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Next, the eight kinds of correct practice are distinguished individually.
Within the text, the eight kinds of wrong practice are subsequently distinguished again;
this serves to reveal the correct practice by means of citing the wrong.
Regarding the first explanation of retrogression and loss, there are four propositions.
First, as for that which causes the intellect to regress and be lost due to one's own failure to hear [the Dharma]:
if one does not show respect toward those who possess the true Dharma and does not go personally to listen, although this constitutes no offense, it still results in such a loss.
However, because one does not listen [to the teachings] and lacks resolute conviction, one is said to have a loss.
Second, regarding the loss of wisdom due to not causing others to hear:
it occurs when others go elsewhere to listen.
Having already been overcome by lack of faith, one thereby commits transgressions;
even if such a mind were absent,
one would simply not allow others to hear [the teaching].
They turn those listeners toward their own false teachings;
for this reason, [the listeners] fall away.
Third, regarding the falling away of wisdom due to obstacles to hearing:
Because one personally does not wish to hear or uphold [the teachings],
one creates obstacles for others to listen and hear them;
by this, one commits an offense.
There is no such intention; rather,
it is solely due to one's own indolence and laziness that obstructs others from hearing the Dharma,
and for this reason, they fall away.
Fourth, there is hearing based on false attachment;
because one does not perceive virtues through cultivation,
one takes mere verbal discourse to be the ultimate.
Due to such transgressions,
even if one does not cling to what has been heard as being ultimate,
if one merely hears it without practicing, wisdom will not be realized.
This is called "retrogression.
Regarding the second interpretation, "forgetting right mindfulness," there are likewise four propositions.
In the first proposition, the phrase "due to karmic obstructions" and so forth means:
It is solely due to karmic obstructions that one forgets when censuring another for an offense;
furthermore, there is no transgression of speech through forgetfulness,
yet there is the forgetting and confusion regarding the fundamental offenses themselves.
Regarding the second explanation— that confusion regarding the training rules causes the loss of mindfulness and so forth—
it means that because one does not correctly receive the instructions from the teacher,
this confusion acts as an obstacle to the cultivation of the three trainings.
Therefore, it is said: "Because it is manifested by the crookedness of false views that do not accord with intrinsic nature.
As for the phrase "due to karmic obstructions" and so forth, it further explains that this is also due to the improper reception [of experience] caused by karmic obstructions.
Although there is no distorted view, it constitutes confusion;
furthermore, it obstructs the cultivation of the three trainings and causes their loss.
Regarding the statement that it "causes the loss of mindfulness regarding the superior understanding and correct practice concerning the Mahāyāna," and so forth:
There are those who have resolved their minds on awakening, studying the Mahāyāna and practicing the Mahāyāna path,
yet they speak to others or to anyone else, saying that there is no distinction between the three vehicles.
Because a bodhisattva fails to give rise to reverence and conceals their actual virtues, they thereby commit a transgression.
Regarding the phrase "due to karmic obstructions" and so forth:
although there may be no lack of respect or concealment of a bodhisattva’s virtues, a transgression still occurs.
However, due to karmic obstructions, the loss of mindfulness leads one to say that the three vehicles are without distinction;
because this obstruction arises, there is forgetfulness.
The fourth [point] states that through confusion, the hidden places are revealed, causing the loss of mindfulness and so forth.
The previous statement— that there is confusion regarding the person who preaches the Dharma, which reveals that they possess something hidden—
arises because one does not wish others to study the Mahāyāna and so forth under that Dharma-preacher.
Therefore, it is said that those faults arise from this transgression.
Regarding the phrase "due to karmic obstructions" and so forth:
although one may have spoken of another's faults without intentional malice, such speech constitutes a transgression.

This occurs directly because, due to karmic obstructions, one forgets within the mind; thus, while speaking of faults in a person who expounds the Dharma, one commits an offense through that state of mental forgetfulness.
Third, the explanation of the four lines concerning the destruction of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).

The initial statement—that one who, out of attachment to their own narrow and limited benefit, does not turn away from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) despite hearing the teachings and so forth, thereby commits an infraction—refers to what was stated above: namely, the superior power of competing with others.
Therefore, the arising of various pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) is not due to preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
As for the statement "because one cannot attain [them]," etc.,
this explains the cause of transgression.
Because they have not yet attained superior, wholesome, and pure dharmas, they take pleasure in their own interests and engage in disputes with others.

They become lax and negligent regarding what they have heard and received, and they now lose all the inferior and middling pure dharmas previously attained; this is called "retrogression from what has been attained."
Second, it should be understood that one destroys the pure, bright dharmas through the fault of defiled craving.
Third, [one does so] through the fault of wrong views, and so forth, up to "thereby committing a transgression."
This contains two types: first, slandering the correct; second, adhering to the false.
As stated in the treatise above: "There are two kinds of evil views:
first, slandering those who uphold the Dharma of the Correct; second, adhering to the false as being correct."
Regarding the statement that one incurs decline through improper conduct:
this refers to the result of decline obtained by slandering what is correct.
Regarding the statement that one incurs decline through deceiving others: [this refers to the result of decline obtained by such deception].
This results in the fruit of decline due to grasping what is wrong as right. Regarding the fourth point,
"due to upholding faults, one destroys the pure dharmas," it was previously stated that this refers to upholding sutras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
